subject: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data

messages.author: af653ea2b39bc54f
messages.subject: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
parts:
Hi, I am a researcher in leopard conservation in South Africa looking at providing population estimates.

I would like to use spatial capture recapture analysis for my data. However, my methodology does not involve camera traps but the collection of direct sightings by professionals guides when on safari. 
 
Here is my first thought:

For the analysis of the direct sighting data, Spatial Capture Recapture method will be adapted as it is normally used for the estimation of population density with camera traps. Each study area will be covered by a grid of 1km2 and the centroid of each grid will be the equivalent of a camera trap location. Each leopard-sighting coordinate recorded will be matched to the coordinate of a grid cell centroid as if the leopard is captured by a camera trap. Is that correct?

SCR requies the following data:

1.      Detectors (is it correct to say the guide is the detector?)

a.      Location (the location of the sighting will be the same as the location of the detector and will not be permanent)

b.      Covariates associated (the covariates should be associated with the guides (i.e. years of experience, hours in the field, km driven) but could the covariates be associated with the location (i.e. distance from a watering hole, habitat type?)

2.      Capture history

a.      Number of leopard encounter by each detector in each sampling occasion (i.e. daily game drive)

b.      Animal level covariates (sex and age)

3.      The survey region

a.      Its location and boundary

b.      Spatial covariates (e.g. distance of sighting from settlement such as lodges, distance from water, habitat types)

If you have other suggestions as to how to analyse direct sighting data, I'd love hear. 


Thank you.
Kind regards,
Marine

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
parts:
Hi Marine
To use SECR you will need reliable individual identifications - perhaps by matching photos. Is that what you intend? Number of encounters per grid cell is not enough.

Detection covariates will be associated with the detector = grid cell, not with individual guides, and a measure of effort per grid cell will be useful. Other spatial covariates (distance to water, vegetation etc.) must be recorded  for each pixel in the habitat mask (a map of areas containing the activity centres of potentially sighted leopards); they may be useful as covariates of leopard density.

But first check that you really have individual-level capture-recapture data.
Murray

parts:
Hi Murray,

Thanks I will have a look.

I have another challenge though. The reserves I am working with are reporting incidental sightings instead of reporting their whole survey. This mean I don't have access to monitoring effort. 
One reserve mentioned that they anyway only go where they know there are leopards so the way they drive is not random. Another reserve only want to record sighting after the drive as they only have one Ipad and don't want their guides using their mobile phone on drive. They select the location after the drive. I have other reserves who have only few sightings and don't do proper game drive but the managers rather have incidental sightings. This is the biggest challenge with this project, each reserve has its own limitations.

However, most of the reserves go at least twice a day on game drive so could that be enough to calculate monitoring effort? I still won't know how much of the reserve is covered though. 

Thanks for the help.

Kind regards,
Marine

messages.subject: Re: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
parts:
Hi Marine
It may be that your data stray so far from the assumptions of the statistical methods that applying the methods can only be misleading. This is especially true of the targeted resighting of known leopards at known places: understandable behaviour of guides, but bad for the statistics. The accuracy of locations recorded after the drive wouldn't bother me so much - I assume the drivers know their routes. The models require reliable negative evidence (from sampling across potential habitat) as well as positive sightings.
Sorry to bring bad news!
Murray

parts:
Hi Murray,

Thanks, that's a tough one!

Please may you just confirm, as I am not sure I understood you 100%. If I know that there is at least one vehicle going out every morning and one every afternoon, could I not create a capture history then? If no leopards were sighted and uploaded on the mobile app, then on that session the capture history will be 0. If however I receive data, the capture history will be 1 for that individual. Could that work? That's data that I can easily ask to get recorded. 

When going through literature, I read a couple of papers mentioning the analysis of citizen science data and the problems of having presence-only data. Are you maybe familiar with it? There are a lot of data collected through iNaturalist, iSeeMammals that there should be a relevant way to help with population estimates and to deal with this type of data. 

Sorry for the headache!

Best,
Marine

parts:
Yes, you can construct a capture history, but what does it tell you? The guides maybe able to relocate the same animal day after day, but learn nothing new about the number and distribution of leopards elsewhere, as needed to fit a model that includes area-wide density as a parameter.

I'm not up on presence-only models, but I imagine they are used to estimate distribution not density.

Le lundi 12 décembre 2022 à 08:11:05 UTC+1, murray...@gmail.com a écrit :
Hi Marine
To use SECR you will need reliable individual identifications - perhaps by matching photos. Is that what you intend? Number of encounters per grid cell is not enough.

Detection covariates will be associated with the detector = grid cell, not with individual guides, and a measure of effort per grid cell will be useful. Other spatial covariates (distance to water, vegetation etc.) must be recorded  for each pixel in the habitat mask (a map of areas containing the activity centres of potentially sighted leopards); they may be useful as covariates of leopard density.

But first check that you really have individual-level capture-recapture data.
Murray

Hi, I am a researcher in leopard conservation in South Africa looking at providing population estimates.

I would like to use spatial capture recapture analysis for my data. However, my methodology does not involve camera traps but the collection of direct sightings by professionals guides when on safari. 
 
Here is my first thought:

For the analysis of the direct sighting data, Spatial Capture Recapture method will be adapted as it is normally used for the estimation of population density with camera traps. Each study area will be covered by a grid of 1km2 and the centroid of each grid will be the equivalent of a camera trap location. Each leopard-sighting coordinate recorded will be matched to the coordinate of a grid cell centroid as if the leopard is captured by a camera trap. Is that correct?

SCR requies the following data:

1.      Detectors (is it correct to say the guide is the detector?)

a.      Location (the location of the sighting will be the same as the location of the detector and will not be permanent)

b.      Covariates associated (the covariates should be associated with the guides (i.e. years of experience, hours in the field, km driven) but could the covariates be associated with the location (i.e. distance from a watering hole, habitat type?)

2.      Capture history

a.      Number of leopard encounter by each detector in each sampling occasion (i.e. daily game drive)

b.      Animal level covariates (sex and age)

3.      The survey region

a.      Its location and boundary

b.      Spatial covariates (e.g. distance of sighting from settlement such as lodges, distance from water, habitat types)

If you have other suggestions as to how to analyse direct sighting data, I'd love hear. 


Thank you.
Kind regards,
Marine

Yes, you can construct a capture history, but what does it tell you? The guides maybe able to relocate the same animal day after day, but learn nothing new about the number and distribution of leopards elsewhere, as needed to fit a model that includes area-wide density as a parameter.

I'm not up on presence-only models, but I imagine they are used to estimate distribution not density.

Le lundi 23 janvier 2023 à 21:43:57 UTC+1, murray...@gmail.com a écrit :
Hi Marine
It may be that your data stray so far from the assumptions of the statistical methods that applying the methods can only be misleading. This is especially true of the targeted resighting of known leopards at known places: understandable behaviour of guides, but bad for the statistics. The accuracy of locations recorded after the drive wouldn't bother me so much - I assume the drivers know their routes. The models require reliable negative evidence (from sampling across potential habitat) as well as positive sightings.
Sorry to bring bad news!
Murray
